reminder: An integer is a whole number: zero, a positive whole number or the negative of one.
definition: The integers $\mathbb Z=\{\dots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\dots\}$ are the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) together with their negatives. The sum, difference and product of two integers are again integers.
examples: $-7$, $0$ and $42$ are integers.
Every [natural number](c:natural-number) is an integer.
Non-example: $1/2$ is not an integer, because it lies strictly between $0$ and $1$.

steps: Take an integer $n$ and write it as the quotient $n/1$.
The denominator $1$ is not zero, so $n/1$ is a [rational number](c:rational-number).
Different integers give different quotients, so the integers sit inside the rational numbers.
links.why: Facts about rational numbers, such as addition and order, apply to integers without change.

steps: Take the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) with their addition and multiplication.
Add a negative $-n$ for each positive natural number $n$, so that $n+(-n)=0$.
Subtraction $a-b$ now always has an answer, and the old operations stay the same.
links.why: It shows that the integers extend the natural numbers by a subtraction that always works.

reminder: The least upper bound of a subset is an upper bound that lies below every other upper bound.
definition: Let $S$ be a [subset](c:subset) of a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order). An element $s$ is the least upper bound of $S$ when $s$ is an [upper bound](c:upper-bound) of $S$ and $s\le u$ for every upper bound $u$ of $S$. It is unique when it exists, and one writes it $\sup S$ or $\bigvee S$.
examples: In $\mathbb R$, the set $\{x : x<1\}$ has least upper bound $1$, and $1$ is not in the set.
For subsets of a set ordered by inclusion, the least upper bound of a family of subsets is their union.
In the positive integers ordered by divisibility, the least upper bound of $4$ and $6$ is $12$.
Non-example: The set $\{x\in\mathbb Q : x^2<2\}$ has no least upper bound in $\mathbb Q$, because $\sqrt2$ is not rational.

steps: Take the least upper bound $s$ of a subset $S$.
By definition $s$ lies above every element of $S$, so $s$ is an [upper bound](c:upper-bound) of $S$.
The special case adds one condition: $s$ lies below every other upper bound of $S$.
links.why: It shows that a least upper bound is the best choice among all upper bounds.

reminder: A local ring is a commutative ring that has exactly one maximal ideal.
definition: A [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ with $1\ne0$ is local when it has exactly one [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak m$. Equivalently, the elements of $R$ outside $\mathfrak m$ are exactly the units of $R$.
examples: Every [field](c:field) is local: its only maximal ideal is $\{0\}$.
The ring $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ of fractions $a/b$ with $p\nmid b$ is local, with maximal ideal $p\mathbb Z_{(p)}$.
The ring $k[[x]]$ of formal power series over a field $k$ is local, with maximal ideal $(x)$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z$ is not local, because $(2)$ and $(3)$ are different maximal ideals.

steps: Take a local ring $R$; it is a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) by definition.
The special case adds one condition: $R$ has exactly one [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal).
Every proper ideal of $R$ then lies inside that maximal ideal.
links.why: Results on commutative rings apply to local rings, and locality adds the unique maximal ideal.

steps: Take a [field](c:field) $k$ as a commutative ring.
The only proper ideal of $k$ is $\{0\}$, so $\{0\}$ is the unique maximal ideal.
Hence $k$ is a local ring whose only non-unit is $0$.
links.why: It shows that a local ring behaves like a field once the maximal ideal is cut out.

steps: A [discrete valuation ring](c:discrete-valuation-ring) $R$ has an element $\pi$ such that every nonzero element is a unit times $\pi^n$.
The non-units are exactly the multiples of $\pi$, and these form the ideal $(\pi)$.
This ideal is the only maximal ideal, because every element outside it is a unit.
links.why: It gives local rings a family of well-understood examples.

reminder: A measurable set belongs to the chosen sigma-algebra, so a measure can give it a size.
definition: Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a [measurable space](c:measurable-space), that is, a set $X$ with a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\Sigma$ of subsets of $X$. A [subset](c:subset) $A\subseteq X$ is measurable when $A\in\Sigma$.
examples: In $\mathbb R$ with the Borel sigma-algebra, every open interval is measurable.
In a set $X$ with the sigma-algebra of all subsets, every subset is measurable.
In a set $X$ with the sigma-algebra $\{\emptyset,X\}$, only $\emptyset$ and $X$ are measurable.
Non-example: A Vitali set, built with the axiom of choice, is not Lebesgue measurable.

steps: Give a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets.
A [Borel set](c:borel-set) is a set in this sigma-algebra.
So every Borel set is a measurable set of $X$ with its Borel sigma-algebra.
links.why: It shows that a topology gives a standard supply of measurable sets.

reminder: A measure gives every measurable set a size from zero to infinity, and sizes of countably many disjoint sets add.
definition: A measure on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $(X,\Sigma)$ is a function $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ into the [extended real numbers](c:extended-real-number) with $\mu(\emptyset)=0$. It is countably additive: $\mu\big(\bigcup_n A_n\big)=\sum_n\mu(A_n)$ for every sequence of pairwise disjoint [measurable sets](c:measurable-set) $A_n$.
examples: The counting measure gives each finite set its number of elements and each infinite set the value $\infty$.
The Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ gives an interval $[a,b]$ the size $b-a$.
A probability measure is a measure $\mu$ with $\mu(X)=1$.
Non-example: The function that sends each finite subset of $\mathbb N$ to the square of its size is not a measure, because it is not additive on disjoint sets.

steps: Take a [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on $(X,\Sigma)$.
Add one condition: the whole space has size one, $\mu(X)=1$.
Then $\mu$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure), and the sizes of events are probabilities.
links.why: It shows that probability is the case of a measure with total size one.

steps: Take any set $X$ with the sigma-algebra of all its subsets.
Set $\mu(A)$ to the number of elements of $A$, and to $\infty$ when $A$ is infinite.
This function is countably additive, so it is a measure, the [counting measure](c:counting-measure).
links.why: It gives the simplest example of a measure on any set.

steps: Start with the length $b-a$ of each interval $[a,b]$ of $\mathbb R$.
Extend the length to all Lebesgue measurable sets by the Carathéodory construction.
The extension is countably additive, so it is the [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure), a measure on $\mathbb R$.
links.why: It shows that length on the real line is a measure.

reminder: A real number is a point of the complete ordered field that contains the rational numbers.
definition: The real numbers $\mathbb R$ form an [ordered field](c:ordered-field) that is [complete](c:completeness): every nonempty set with an upper bound has a [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound). This field is unique up to a unique order-preserving field isomorphism, and it contains the [rational numbers](c:rational-number).
examples: $2$, $-\tfrac13$, $\sqrt2$ and $\pi$ are real numbers.
Every [Dedekind cut](c:dedekind-cut) of the rational numbers gives exactly one real number.
Every [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) of real numbers has a real limit.
Non-example: $\sqrt{-1}$ is not a real number, because no real number has a negative square.

steps: Take the [rational numbers](c:rational-number), an ordered field with gaps such as $\sqrt2$.
Fill the gaps by adding limits of Cauchy sequences, or by using Dedekind cuts.
The result is a complete ordered field, the real numbers, and it contains the rationals.
links.why: It shows that the real numbers are the rationals with the gaps filled.

steps: Take a [complex number](c:complex-number) $z=a+bi$ with $a$ and $b$ real.
Require that the imaginary part $b$ is $0$.
Then $z=a$ is a real number, and addition and multiplication agree with those of $\mathbb R$.
links.why: It shows that real numbers are the complex numbers that lie on the real axis.

reminder: A measure is sigma-finite when the whole space is a countable union of sets of finite measure.
definition: A [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $(X,\Sigma)$ is sigma-finite when $X=\bigcup_n A_n$ for countably many [measurable sets](c:measurable-set) $A_n$ with $\mu(A_n)<\infty$ for every $n$. The sets $A_n$ can always be chosen to increase with $n$.
examples: The Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ is sigma-finite, because $\mathbb R$ is the union of the intervals $[-n,n]$ of finite length.
Every [finite measure](c:finite-measure), such as a probability measure, is sigma-finite.
The counting measure on a countable set is sigma-finite.
Non-example: The counting measure on $\mathbb R$ is not sigma-finite, because a countable union of finite sets is countable.

steps: Take a [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on $(X,\Sigma)$.
Add one condition: $X$ is a countable union of measurable sets of finite measure.
The condition holds for every finite measure, but it fails for the counting measure on an uncountable set.
links.why: It shows which extra condition lets one use theorems that need sets of finite size, such as Fubini's theorem.

steps: Take a [finite measure](c:finite-measure) $\mu$, so that $\mu(X)<\infty$.
Put $A_n=X$ for every $n$.
Then $X=\bigcup_n A_n$ and every $\mu(A_n)$ is finite, so $\mu$ is sigma-finite.
links.why: It shows that every finite measure, and so every probability measure, is sigma-finite.

reminder: An ultrafilter is a proper filter that contains, for every subset, the subset or its complement.
definition: An ultrafilter on a set $X$ is a [filter](c:filter) $\mathcal U$ of subsets of $X$ with $\emptyset\notin\mathcal U$ such that for every [subset](c:subset) $A\subseteq X$ either $A\in\mathcal U$ or $X\setminus A\in\mathcal U$. Equivalently, it is a maximal proper filter on the [power set](c:power-set) of $X$.
examples: For a point $x\in X$, the family of all subsets that contain $x$ is an ultrafilter, called principal.
On an infinite set, a non-principal ultrafilter contains no finite set, and its existence needs the axiom of choice.
Non-example: The filter of cofinite subsets of $\mathbb N$ is not an ultrafilter, because neither the even numbers nor the odd numbers belong to it.

steps: Take a proper [filter](c:filter) $\mathcal F$ on the [power set](c:power-set) of $X$.
Add one condition: for every subset $A$, either $A$ or $X\setminus A$ lies in $\mathcal F$.
This condition is equivalent to maximality, because no proper filter is strictly larger.
links.why: It shows that an ultrafilter is a filter that cannot be enlarged.

reminder: The variance of a random variable is the mean of its squared distance from its own mean.
definition: For a real [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ with finite second moment, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[(X-E[X])^2]$, where $E$ is the [expected value](c:expected-value). It measures how far $X$ spreads around its mean, and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2$.
examples: A fair coin with $X=1$ for heads and $X=0$ for tails has $\mathrm{Var}(X)=1/4$.
A constant random variable has variance $0$.
A roll of a fair die has variance $35/12$.
Non-example: A Cauchy random variable has no finite variance, because $E[X^2]$ is infinite.

steps: Take a random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ with its [covariance matrix](c:covariance-matrix), whose entries are $\mathrm{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$.
Let $n=1$, so that the vector is the single [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$.
The matrix is then the $1\times1$ matrix with the entry $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.
links.why: It shows that variance is the one-dimensional case of the covariance matrix.

reminder: An analytic function equals a convergent power series near every point of its domain.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f$ on an [open set](c:open-set) $U$ is analytic when for every $a\in U$ there are coefficients $c_n$ and a radius $r>0$ with $f(x)=\sum_n c_n(x-a)^n$ for $|x-a|<r$. The [power series](c:power-series) can change from point to point.
examples: Polynomials, $e^x$, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are analytic on $\mathbb R$.
The function $1/(1+x^2)$ is analytic on $\mathbb R$, although its Taylor series at $0$ converges only for $|x|<1$.
Non-example: The function $e^{-1/x^2}$ with value $0$ at $0$ is smooth but not analytic at $0$, because all its derivatives vanish there and the function is not zero near $0$.

steps: Take an analytic function $f$ with $f(x)=\sum_n c_n(x-a)^n$ near $a$.
A power series can be differentiated term by term inside its radius of convergence.
So every derivative of $f$ exists near $a$, and $f$ is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function).
The special case adds that $f$ agrees with its Taylor series near every point.
links.why: It shows that analytic functions are smooth, and that smoothness alone does not give a power series.

steps: A [polynomial](c:polynomial) is a power series with only finitely many nonzero coefficients.
Such a series converges for every $x$, so the polynomial equals its own power series everywhere.
Hence every polynomial is an analytic function on $\mathbb R$.
links.why: It shows that polynomials are the simplest analytic functions.

reminder: A bijection pairs every element of the domain with exactly one element of the codomain, and no element is missed.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:A\to B$ is a bijection when it is an [injection](c:injection), so different elements have different images, and a [surjection](c:surjection), so every element of $B$ is an image. Then $f$ has an [inverse](c:inverse) function $f^{-1}:B\to A$, which is also a bijection.
examples: The function $x\mapsto2x+1$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$ is a bijection.
The identity function on any set is a bijection.
The map $n\mapsto2n$ is a bijection from $\mathbb N$ onto the even natural numbers.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^2$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$ is not a bijection, because $x$ and $-x$ have the same image and negative numbers are never reached.

steps: In the category of sets, the objects are sets and the morphisms are functions.
A bijection $f$ has an inverse function $g$ with $g\circ f$ and $f\circ g$ equal to the identities.
So $f$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) of sets, and every isomorphism of sets is a bijection.
links.why: It shows that a bijection is an isomorphism in the category of sets.

steps: Take a set $X$ and a bijection $f:X\to X$ with the same domain and codomain.
Call $f$ a [permutation](c:permutation) of $X$.
The special case adds that the domain and the codomain are the same set.
links.why: It shows that a permutation is a bijection of a set onto itself.

steps: Take a bijection $f:X\to Y$ between [topological spaces](c:topological-space).
Add the condition that $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are continuous.
Then $f$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism).
links.why: It shows that a homeomorphism is a bijection that respects the topology in both directions.

reminder: A computable function is a function that some algorithm can calculate on every input.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:\mathbb N^k\to\mathbb N$ is computable when some [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) halts on every input $(n_1,\dots,n_k)$ of [natural numbers](c:natural-number) with the output $f(n_1,\dots,n_k)$. The same class of functions results from recursive functions and from the lambda calculus.
examples: Addition, multiplication and the function that gives the $n$th prime number are computable.
Every polynomial with integer coefficients, read as a function on $\mathbb N$, is computable.
Non-example: The halting function, which is $1$ when machine number $e$ halts on input $e$ and $0$ otherwise, is not computable.

steps: A [partial computable function](c:partial-computable-function) is computed by a Turing machine that may run forever on some inputs.
Take such a function whose machine halts on every input.
Then the function is defined everywhere, and it is a computable function.
links.why: It shows that computable functions are the everywhere-defined partial computable functions.

reminder: The exponential function is the function that equals its own derivative and has the value one at zero.
definition: The exponential function is the sum of the [power series](c:power-series) $\exp(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/n!$ for every [real number](c:real-number) $x$. It is the only function that equals its own [derivative](c:derivative) and has value $1$ at $0$, and it satisfies $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$.
examples: $\exp(0)=1$ and $\exp(1)=e\approx2.718$.
The solution of $y'=ky$ with $y(0)=y_0$ is $y_0\exp(kx)$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto2^x$ is not the exponential function, because its derivative is $\ln 2\cdot2^x$ and not $2^x$.

steps: The [matrix exponential](c:matrix-exponential) of a square matrix $A$ is $\sum_{n\ge0}A^n/n!$.
Take $1\times1$ matrices, which are just real numbers $x$.
Then $A^n=x^n$, and the sum is $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/n!=\exp(x)$.
links.why: It shows that the real exponential is the one-dimensional case of the matrix exponential.

reminder: A finite field is a field with finitely many elements, and its size is a prime power.
definition: A finite field is a [field](c:field) whose set of elements is a [finite set](c:finite-set). Its size is a [prime power](c:prime-power) $p^n$, where $p$ is its characteristic, and two finite fields of the same size are isomorphic, so one writes $\mathbb F_{p^n}$.
examples: For a prime $p$, the integers modulo $p$ form the finite field $\mathbb F_p$.
The set $\{0,1,a,a+1\}$ with $a^2=a+1$ and $2=0$ is the field $\mathbb F_4$ with four elements.
There is no field with six elements, because six is not a prime power.
Non-example: The integers modulo $6$ are not a field, because $2\cdot3=0$ although $2$ and $3$ are not zero.

steps: Start with a [field](c:field) $F$.
Add one condition: the set $F$ has finitely many elements.
Then $F$ has prime characteristic $p$, and $|F|=p^n$ for some $n\ge1$.
links.why: It shows what the finiteness condition forces: a prime characteristic and a prime power size.

steps: The [prime field](c:prime-field) of characteristic $p$ is the subfield generated by $1$.
It consists of the integers modulo $p$, so it has $p$ elements.
So $\mathbb F_p$ is a finite field, the case $n=1$ of $\mathbb F_{p^n}$.
links.why: It shows that the integers modulo a prime are the smallest finite fields.

reminder: A Haar measure is a nonzero measure on a locally compact group that is the same after every left translation.
definition: Let $G$ be a [locally compact group](c:locally-compact-group). A Haar measure on $G$ is a nonzero [Radon measure](c:radon-measure) $\mu$ that is left invariant: $\mu(gA)=\mu(A)$ for every [Borel set](c:borel-set) $A$ and every $g\in G$. It exists and is unique up to a positive constant factor.
examples: The Lebesgue measure is a Haar measure on the group $(\mathbb R^n,+)$.
The counting measure is a Haar measure on every discrete group.
The arc-length measure is a Haar measure on the circle group.
Non-example: The Lebesgue measure on the multiplicative group $(0,\infty)$ is not left invariant, because multiplying by $g$ scales lengths by $g$; the Haar measure there is $dx/x$.

steps: Take a [locally compact group](c:locally-compact-group) $G$ and a [Radon measure](c:radon-measure) $\mu$ on it.
Add the condition that $\mu$ is nonzero and invariant under left translation by each $g\in G$.
Such a $\mu$ is a Haar measure, and it is unique up to a positive scalar.
links.why: It shows that a Haar measure is a Radon measure that respects the group structure.

steps: Take the group $(\mathbb R^n,+)$, which is a [locally compact group](c:locally-compact-group).
The [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) is nonzero and Radon.
It is invariant under every translation $x\mapsto x+g$, so it is a Haar measure of $\mathbb R^n$.
links.why: It shows that Lebesgue measure is the Haar measure of the additive group of $\mathbb R^n$.

reminder: A homotopy equivalence is a continuous map that has a continuous inverse up to homotopy.
definition: A [continuous function](c:continuous-function) $f:X\to Y$ is a homotopy equivalence when there is a continuous $g:Y\to X$ such that $g\circ f$ is [homotopic](c:homotopy) to the [identity function](c:identity-function) of $X$ and $f\circ g$ is homotopic to the identity of $Y$. Then $X$ and $Y$ have the same homotopy type.
examples: The inclusion of a point into a [convex set](c:convex-set) is a homotopy equivalence.
The inclusion of the circle $S^1$ into the punctured plane $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ is a homotopy equivalence.
Every homeomorphism is a homotopy equivalence.
Non-example: The inclusion of a point into the circle $S^1$ is not a homotopy equivalence, because $S^1$ cannot be shrunk to a point.

steps: Take a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $f:X\to Y$ with continuous inverse $g$.
Then $g\circ f$ and $f\circ g$ are equal to the identities.
A constant homotopy shows that they are homotopic to the identities, so $f$ is a homotopy equivalence.
links.why: It shows that a homeomorphism is the strictest kind of homotopy equivalence.

steps: Take a homotopy equivalence $f:X\to Y$ with homotopy inverse $g$.
Homotopic maps induce the same maps on homotopy groups, up to a change of base point.
So $f$ induces an isomorphism on every homotopy group, and $f$ is a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence).
links.why: It shows that homotopy equivalences are weak homotopy equivalences, and that the reverse needs extra conditions.

steps: A [deformation retract](c:deformation-retract) $A\subseteq X$ has a homotopy from the identity of $X$ to a retraction $r:X\to A$.
The inclusion $i:A\to X$ then satisfies $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}_A$ and $i\circ r\simeq\mathrm{id}_X$.
So the inclusion is a homotopy equivalence with inverse $r$.
links.why: It shows that a deformation retraction is a homotopy equivalence with an especially simple inverse.

reminder: An interval is a set of real numbers that contains every number between any two of its elements.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $I$ of the [real numbers](c:real-number) is an interval when $a,b\in I$ and $a<c<b$ imply $c\in I$, using the [total order](c:total-order) of $\mathbb R$. Each nonempty interval has endpoints $a\le b$ in $[-\infty,\infty]$, and it may contain either endpoint when that endpoint is finite.
examples: $(0,1)$, $[0,1]$ and $[0,\infty)$ are intervals.
The whole line $\mathbb R$ and every single point $\{x\}$ are intervals.
Non-example: $[0,1]\cup[2,3]$ is not an interval, because $1.5$ lies between $1$ and $2$ but not in the set.

steps: Take real numbers $a\le b$.
The set $[a,b]=\{x : a\le x\le b\}$ contains every number between two of its elements.
So the [closed interval](c:closed-interval) $[a,b]$ is an interval that contains both endpoints.
links.why: It shows that a closed interval is an interval with both endpoints included.

steps: A [convex set](c:convex-set) in $\mathbb R$ contains the segment between any two of its points.
In $\mathbb R$ the segment between $a$ and $b$ is the set of numbers between $a$ and $b$.
So a subset of $\mathbb R$ is an interval exactly when it is convex.
links.why: It shows that intervals are the convex sets of the real line.

reminder: An isometry is a map between metric spaces that keeps every distance the same.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:X\to Y$ between [metric spaces](c:metric-space) is an isometry when $d_Y(f(x),f(y))=d_X(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$. Every isometry is injective and continuous, and its inverse on the image is again an isometry.
examples: Translations and rotations of the Euclidean plane are isometries.
The inclusion of a subspace into a metric space is an isometry for the restricted metric.
Non-example: The map $x\mapsto2x$ on $\mathbb R$ is not an isometry, because it doubles every distance.

steps: Take an isometry $f$, so that $d(f(x),f(y))=d(x,y)$.
Then $d(f(x),f(y))\le1\cdot d(x,y)$, which is the Lipschitz condition with constant $1$.
So $f$ is a [Lipschitz continuous function](c:lipschitz-continuous-function), and the special case adds equality.
links.why: It shows that isometries are continuous, with the best possible Lipschitz constant.

steps: Take two normed spaces and a [linear map](c:linear-map) $T$ between them.
Add the condition $\lVert Tx\rVert=\lVert x\rVert$ for every $x$.
Then $d(Tx,Ty)=\lVert T(x-y)\rVert=d(x,y)$, so $T$ is an isometry for the metrics given by the norms.
links.why: It shows that a linear isometry is an isometry that is also linear.

reminder: A meromorphic function is holomorphic everywhere except at isolated poles.
definition: A function $f$ on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ is meromorphic when there is a discrete set $P\subseteq U$ such that $f$ is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on $U\setminus P$ and has a [pole](c:pole) at each point of $P$. Near a pole, $f$ has a [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) with finitely many negative powers.
examples: Every [rational function](c:rational-function), such as $1/(z^2+1)$, is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$.
The function $\tan z$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$, with poles at the points $\pi/2+k\pi$.
Non-example: $e^{1/z}$ is not meromorphic at $0$, because $0$ is an essential singularity and not a pole.

steps: Take a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f$ on an open set $U$.
Take the empty set as the set of poles, which is discrete in $U$.
Then $f$ is holomorphic off the empty set, so $f$ is meromorphic.
links.why: It shows that meromorphic functions allow poles on top of the holomorphic functions.

steps: Write a [rational function](c:rational-function) as $p/q$ in lowest terms, with polynomials $p$ and $q$.
Then $q$ has finitely many zeros, and the quotient is holomorphic away from them.
At each zero of $q$ the quotient has a pole, so the function is meromorphic.
links.why: It shows that rational functions are the meromorphic functions that polynomials build.

reminder: A metric space is a set with a distance function that is symmetric, positive and obeys the triangle inequality.
definition: A metric space is a [set](c:set) $X$ with a function $d:X\times X\to[0,\infty)$ into the [real numbers](c:real-number) such that $d(x,y)=0$ exactly when $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. The function $d$ is called the metric.
examples: The real line with $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ is a metric space.
The plane with the straight-line distance is a metric space, and so is the plane with $d(x,y)=|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|$.
Every set with the discrete metric, where $d(x,y)=1$ for $x\ne y$, is a metric space.
Non-example: On $\mathbb R$ the function $d(x,y)=(x-y)^2$ is not a metric, because $d(0,2)=4$ is larger than $d(0,1)+d(1,2)=2$.

steps: Take the open balls of the metric as a base.
Call a set open when it is a union of open balls.
These open sets form a [topological space](c:topological-space), the metric topology of the metric space.
links.why: It shows that every metric space carries a topology, so topological results apply to it.

steps: Take a [normed space](c:normed-space) with norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert$.
Define the distance of two vectors as $d(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert$.
This $d$ is symmetric, is zero exactly on equal points and obeys the triangle inequality, so it is a metric.
links.why: It shows that every norm gives a metric, and that normed spaces are metric spaces.

reminder: In modular arithmetic, two integers count as equal when their difference is divisible by the modulus.
definition: Fix an [integer](c:integer) $n\ge1$ and call $a$ and $b$ congruent modulo $n$, written $a\equiv b\pmod n$, when $n$ [divides](c:divisibility) $a-b$. Modular arithmetic adds and multiplies the [equivalence classes](c:equivalence-class) of this relation, and these classes form $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$.
examples: Modulo $12$, $9+5\equiv2$, which is the arithmetic of a clock.
Modulo $7$, $3\cdot5=15\equiv1$, so $5$ is the inverse of $3$.
Two integers are congruent modulo $2$ exactly when they are both even or both odd.
Non-example: $5$ and $8$ are not congruent modulo $4$, because $4$ does not divide $5-8=-3$.

steps: Take the ring $\mathbb Z$ and its [ideal](c:ideal) $n\mathbb Z$ of all multiples of $n$.
The [quotient ring](c:quotient-ring) $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ has the cosets $a+n\mathbb Z$ as elements.
Two integers lie in the same coset exactly when they are congruent modulo $n$, so the cosets are the classes of modular arithmetic.
links.why: It shows that modular arithmetic is the quotient ring of the integers by the multiples of $n$.

reminder: The orbit of a point is the set of all points to which the group moves it.
definition: Let a [group](c:group) $G$ act on a set $X$ by a [group action](c:group-action). The orbit of a point $x\in X$ is the set $G\cdot x=\{g\cdot x : g\in G\}$. Two orbits are equal or disjoint, so the orbits partition $X$.
examples: The rotations of the plane about $0$ act on the plane, and the orbit of a point $x\ne0$ is the circle through $x$ centred at $0$.
The symmetric group $S_n$ acting on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ has just one orbit.
When a group acts on itself by conjugation, the orbits are the conjugacy classes.
Non-example: The subset $\{1,2\}$ is not an orbit of $S_3$ acting on $\{1,2,3\}$, because the orbit of $1$ is all of $\{1,2,3\}$.

steps: Define $x\sim y$ when $y=g\cdot x$ for some $g\in G$.
This relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, because $G$ has an identity, inverses and products.
The [equivalence class](c:equivalence-class) of $x$ for this relation is exactly its orbit $G\cdot x$.
links.why: It shows that the orbits of an action are the classes of one equivalence relation.

steps: Let $G$ act on itself by conjugation, $g\cdot x=gxg^{-1}$.
This is a [group action](c:group-action).
The orbit of $x$ is $\{gxg^{-1} : g\in G\}$, which is the [conjugacy class](c:conjugacy-class) of $x$.
links.why: It shows that conjugacy classes are the orbits of the conjugation action.

reminder: A paracompact space is a Hausdorff space in which every open cover has a locally finite open refinement.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is paracompact when it is a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) and every [open cover](c:open-cover) of $X$ has an open [refinement](c:refinement) that is a [locally finite cover](c:locally-finite-cover). Locally finite means that each point has a neighbourhood that meets only finitely many sets of the refinement.
examples: Every [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) is paracompact.
Every metric space is paracompact, by Stone's theorem.
Non-example: The long line is Hausdorff and countably compact but not compact, so it is not paracompact.

steps: Take a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) $X$ and an [open cover](c:open-cover) of it.
By compactness the cover has a finite subcover, which is an open refinement of the cover.
A finite cover is locally finite, so $X$ is paracompact.
links.why: It shows that compactness gives paracompactness in the Hausdorff case.

reminder: A partition of unity is a family of continuous functions, each zero outside a small open set, whose sum is the constant function one.
definition: Let $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an [open cover](c:open-cover) of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. A partition of unity subordinate to it is a family of [continuous functions](c:continuous-function) $\varphi_i:X\to[0,1]$ such that the [support](c:support) of each $\varphi_i$ lies in $U_i$, the supports form a [locally finite cover](c:locally-finite-cover), and $\sum_i\varphi_i(x)=1$ for every $x\in X$.
examples: For the cover $\{(-\infty,2),(0,\infty)\}$ of $\mathbb R$, let $\varphi_1$ be $1$ on $(-\infty,\tfrac12]$, $0$ on $[\tfrac32,\infty)$ and linear in between, and let $\varphi_2=1-\varphi_1$.
For the cover $\{X\}$ of one set, the constant function $1$ is a partition of unity.
Every open cover of a paracompact Hausdorff space has a partition of unity subordinate to it.
Non-example: On $\mathbb R$, the constant functions $\varphi_n=2^{-n}$ for $n\ge1$ sum to $1$, but each is nonzero everywhere, so their supports are not small and not locally finite.

steps: Take a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ and an [open cover](c:open-cover) of it.
Ask that every function $\varphi_i$ of the family is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) and not only continuous.
The family is then a [smooth partition of unity](c:smooth-partition-of-unity), a partition of unity with one added condition.
links.why: It shows that a smooth partition of unity is a partition of unity whose functions are smooth.

reminder: An abelian category is an additive category with kernels and cokernels in which every monomorphism and epimorphism is normal.
definition: An abelian category is an [additive category](c:additive-category) in which every morphism has a [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) and a [cokernel](c:cokernel), every monomorphism is the kernel of some morphism, and every epimorphism is the cokernel of some morphism. Then each set of morphisms is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group), and every morphism factors as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism.
examples: The category of abelian groups with group homomorphisms is abelian.
For a ring $R$, the category of left $R$-[modules](c:module) is abelian.
Sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space form an abelian category.
Non-example: Free abelian groups form an additive category that is not abelian, because the monomorphism $2:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ is not the kernel of any morphism.

steps: Start with an [additive category](c:additive-category), which has finite sums and an abelian group structure on each set of morphisms.
Add the condition that every morphism has a kernel and a cokernel.
Add the condition that every monomorphism is a kernel and every epimorphism is a cokernel.
links.why: It shows which conditions turn an additive category into one where homological algebra works.

reminder: A basis is a linearly independent set of vectors that spans the whole space.
definition: A basis of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is a family $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors that is [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) and whose [span](c:span) is $V$. Every vector of $V$ is then a unique finite [linear combination](c:linear-combination) $\sum_i a_ie_i$.
examples: The vectors $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^3$.
The monomials $1,x,x^2,\dots$ form a basis of the space of polynomials.
Over $\mathbb Q$, the numbers $1$ and $\sqrt2$ form a basis of the field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$.
Non-example: The vectors $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$ are not a basis of $\mathbb R^2$, because $(1,1)=(1,0)+(0,1)$ makes them dependent.

steps: Take a basis $B$ of $V$; its span is $V$, so $B$ is a [spanning set](c:spanning-set).
The special case adds that $B$ is [linearly independent](c:linear-independence).
Equivalently, no proper subset of $B$ still spans $V$.
links.why: It shows that a basis is a spanning set with no redundant vector.

steps: Take a finite-dimensional [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) and a family $(e_i)$ with $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$.
Orthonormal vectors are linearly independent, because pairing a vanishing combination with $e_j$ gives the coefficient of $e_j$.
If the family also spans, it is a basis, and the special case adds orthonormality, an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis).
links.why: It shows that an orthonormal basis is a basis with extra conditions that make coordinates easy to compute.

reminder: A theory is consistent when it proves no contradiction.
definition: A [theory](c:theory) $T$ is consistent when no [formal proof](c:formal-proof) from $T$ ends with a [contradiction](c:contradiction) $\bot$. Equivalently, there is no [sentence](c:sentence) $\varphi$ such that $T$ proves both $\varphi$ and $\neg\varphi$.
examples: The theory of groups is consistent, because the integers under addition satisfy its axioms.
Every theory that has a model is consistent.
If Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory is consistent, it cannot prove its own consistency, by Gödel's second incompleteness theorem.
Non-example: The theory $\{P,\neg P\}$ for a sentence $P$ is not consistent, because it proves $P\wedge\neg P$.

reminder: A convex polyhedron is a bounded solid with flat polygon faces that contains every segment between its points.
definition: A convex polyhedron is the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of finitely many points of $\mathbb R^3$ that do not all lie in one plane. It is a bounded [convex set](c:convex-set) whose boundary consists of flat polygons, called faces, that meet in edges and vertices.
examples: A cube and a tetrahedron are convex polyhedra.
Every Platonic solid is a convex polyhedron.
Non-example: A solid L-shaped block is a polyhedron but not convex, because a segment between two of its points can leave the block.

steps: A [convex polytope](c:convex-polytope) in $\mathbb R^n$ is the convex hull of finitely many points.
Take the dimension $n=3$ of ordinary space.
Require the points to span $\mathbb R^3$, so that the solid has a nonempty interior and flat polygon faces.
links.why: It shows that a convex polyhedron is the three-dimensional case of a convex polytope.

steps: A [polyhedron](c:polyhedron) is a solid bounded by flat polygons.
Take a polyhedron $P$ that is also a convex set.
Then every segment between two points of $P$ stays in $P$, and this convexity is the added condition.
links.why: It shows that convexity is the one condition that separates convex polyhedra from general polyhedra.

reminder: A diffeomorphism is a smooth bijection between manifolds whose inverse is also smooth.
definition: A diffeomorphism between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ and $N$ is a [bijection](c:bijection) $f:M\to N$ such that $f$ and its [inverse](c:inverse) $f^{-1}$ are both [smooth maps](c:smooth-map). Its derivative is then invertible at every point, so $M$ and $N$ have the same dimension.
examples: The map $x\mapsto2x+1$ is a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R$.
Every rotation of the plane is a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^2$.
The map $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\ln$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ is a smooth bijection but not a diffeomorphism, because its inverse $x^{1/3}$ is not differentiable at $0$.

steps: Take a diffeomorphism $f:M\to N$ with inverse $f^{-1}$.
Smooth maps are continuous, so $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are continuous.
So $f$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism), and the special case adds that $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth.
links.why: It shows that a diffeomorphism is a homeomorphism that also respects the smooth structure.

steps: In the category of [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold), the morphisms are [smooth maps](c:smooth-map).
An [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) is a smooth map with a smooth two-sided inverse.
That is exactly a diffeomorphism.
links.why: It shows that a diffeomorphism is an isomorphism of smooth manifolds.

reminder: Homology measures the holes of a chain complex by taking cycles modulo boundaries in each degree.
definition: The homology of a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $(C_n,\partial_n)$ of [abelian groups](c:abelian-group) is $H_n=\ker\partial_n/\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}$, the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) of the [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) of $\partial_n$ by the [image](c:image) of $\partial_{n+1}$. It is well defined because $\partial_n\circ\partial_{n+1}=0$, and it vanishes in degree $n$ exactly when the complex is exact there.
examples: The circle has $H_0=\mathbb Z$ and $H_1=\mathbb Z$, where $H_1$ counts the one loop, and $H_n=0$ for $n\ge2$.
The $2$-sphere has $H_2=\mathbb Z$.
An exact complex has zero homology in every degree.
Non-example: A sequence of maps with $\partial_1\circ\partial_2\ne0$ is not a chain complex, so it has no homology.

reminder: A lattice in $\mathbb R^n$ is the set of all integer combinations of a basis of $\mathbb R^n$.
definition: A lattice in $\mathbb R^n$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $\Lambda$ of the [vector space](c:vector-space) $\mathbb R^n$ of the form $\Lambda=\mathbb Zv_1+\dots+\mathbb Zv_n$, where $v_1,\dots,v_n$ is a [basis](c:basis) of $\mathbb R^n$. Equivalently, $\Lambda$ is a discrete subgroup that spans $\mathbb R^n$.
examples: $\mathbb Z^n$ is a lattice in $\mathbb R^n$.
The Gaussian integers $\mathbb Z[i]$ form a lattice in $\mathbb C=\mathbb R^2$.
The points $m(1,0)+n(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)$ with $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ form the hexagonal lattice in the plane.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z+\sqrt2\,\mathbb Z$ is a subgroup of $\mathbb R$ but not a lattice, because it is dense and so not discrete.

steps: Take the group $(\mathbb R^n,+)$ and a lattice $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^n$.
The set $\Lambda$ is closed under addition and negation, so it is a [subgroup](c:subgroup).
The special case adds that $\Lambda$ is discrete and spans $\mathbb R^n$.
links.why: It shows that a lattice is a subgroup of the vector space with two extra conditions.

steps: The $E_8$ lattice is spanned over $\mathbb Z$ by eight linearly independent vectors of $\mathbb R^8$.
So it is the set of integer combinations of a basis of $\mathbb R^8$, and hence a lattice.
The special case adds that all inner products are integers and all squared lengths are even, with covolume $1$.
links.why: It shows that the $E_8$ lattice is a lattice with an especially symmetric inner product.

reminder: A maximal ideal is a proper ideal that no other proper ideal strictly contains.
definition: An [ideal](c:ideal) $\mathfrak m$ of a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is maximal when $\mathfrak m\ne R$ and no ideal $I$ satisfies $\mathfrak m\subsetneq I\subsetneq R$. In a commutative ring with $1$, this holds exactly when $R/\mathfrak m$ is a [field](c:field).
examples: In $\mathbb Z$, the ideal $(p)$ is maximal for every prime $p$.
In the polynomial ring $k[x]$ over a field $k$, the ideal $(x-a)$ is maximal for every $a\in k$.
In a field, $\{0\}$ is the only maximal ideal.
Non-example: The ideal $(4)$ of $\mathbb Z$ is not maximal, because $(4)\subsetneq(2)\subsetneq\mathbb Z$.

steps: Take a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $R$; it is an [ideal](c:ideal).
The special case adds that $\mathfrak m$ is proper.
It also adds that no proper ideal contains $\mathfrak m$ strictly.
links.why: It shows that a maximal ideal is a proper ideal that cannot be enlarged.

steps: Let $\mathfrak m$ be maximal in a commutative ring $R$, and let $ab\in\mathfrak m$ with $a\notin\mathfrak m$.
Then $\mathfrak m+(a)=R$ by maximality, so $1=m+ra$ for some $m\in\mathfrak m$ and $r\in R$.
Multiply by $b$ to get $b=mb+rab\in\mathfrak m$, so $\mathfrak m$ is a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal).
links.why: It shows that in a commutative ring every maximal ideal is prime.

reminder: A topological space is metrizable when some metric on its points gives exactly its topology.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $(X,\tau)$ is metrizable when there is a [metric](c:metric-space) $d$ on $X$ whose [metric topology](c:metric-topology) equals $\tau$. The metric $d$ is not unique, and many different metrics can give the same open sets.
examples: $\mathbb R^n$ with its usual topology is metrizable by the Euclidean metric.
Every discrete space is metrizable by the metric with $d(x,y)=1$ for $x\ne y$.
Non-example: An infinite set with the cofinite topology is not metrizable, because it is not Hausdorff.

steps: Start with a [topological space](c:topological-space) $(X,\tau)$.
Add the condition that some metric $d$ has its open balls as a base of $\tau$.
Then $(X,d)$ is a metric space, and the open sets of $\tau$ are the unions of open balls.
links.why: It shows that metrizability is the condition that a topology comes from a distance.

steps: A [Polish space](c:polish-space) is separable and has a complete metric that gives its topology.
That complete metric is in particular a metric that gives the topology.
So every Polish space is metrizable, and the special case adds separability and completeness.
links.why: It shows that Polish spaces are metrizable spaces with two extra conditions.

reminder: A subsequence keeps infinitely many terms of a sequence in their original order.
definition: Let $(a_n)$ be a [sequence](c:sequence). A subsequence is a sequence $(a_{n_k})_{k\ge1}$, where $n_1<n_2<n_3<\cdots$ is a strictly increasing sequence of [natural numbers](c:natural-number).
examples: The terms $a_2,a_4,a_6,\dots$ with even index form a subsequence of $(a_n)$.
The squares $1,4,9,16,\dots$ form a subsequence of $1,2,3,4,\dots$, with $n_k=k^2$.
Every sequence is a subsequence of itself, with $n_k=k$.
Non-example: The terms $a_2,a_1,a_3,\dots$ do not form a subsequence of $(a_n)$, because the indices $2,1,3,\dots$ do not increase.

reminder: A vector bundle is a family of vector spaces over a base space that looks like a product locally.
definition: A vector bundle of rank $r$ over a [topological space](c:topological-space) $B$ is a continuous map $\pi:E\to B$ whose fibres $\pi^{-1}(b)$ are [vector spaces](c:vector-space), such that every point of $B$ has a neighbourhood $U$ with a [local trivialization](c:local-trivialization). This is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $\pi^{-1}(U)\to U\times\mathbb R^r$ that is linear on each fibre.
examples: The product $B\times\mathbb R^r$ is the trivial vector bundle of rank $r$.
The [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle) of a smooth manifold is a vector bundle.
The Möbius strip is a line bundle over the circle.
Non-example: Over $\mathbb R$, take the fibre $\mathbb R$ at $0$ and the fibre $\{0\}$ at every other point; the fibre dimension jumps, so no local trivialization exists.

steps: Take a [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) $E\to B$ whose fibre is the vector space $\mathbb R^r$.
Require every local trivialization to be linear on each fibre, so that the transition maps lie in $GL_r(\mathbb R)$.
Then $E\to B$ is a vector bundle, a fibre bundle with structure group $GL_r$.
links.why: It shows that a vector bundle is a fibre bundle whose fibres and gluing maps are linear.

steps: Take a vector bundle $E\to B$ of rank $r=1$.
Each fibre is then a one-dimensional vector space, that is, a line.
So $E$ is a [line bundle](c:line-bundle).
links.why: It shows that a line bundle is a vector bundle of rank one.

steps: Take a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ and form the set $TM$ of all tangent vectors.
Each tangent space $T_pM$ is a vector space, and the charts of $M$ give local trivializations.
So $TM\to M$ is a vector bundle, the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle), of rank $\dim M$.
links.why: It shows that the tangent bundle is the vector bundle built from the tangent spaces of a manifold.

reminder: A vector space is an abelian group of vectors that can be scaled by the elements of a field.
definition: A vector space over a [field](c:field) $K$ is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $(V,+)$ with a scalar multiplication $K\times V\to V$. This multiplication is associative, sends $1$ to the identity, and distributes over the addition of $V$ and the addition of $K$.
examples: $\mathbb R^n$ is a vector space over $\mathbb R$.
The polynomials in $x$ with coefficients in $K$ form a vector space over $K$.
The continuous real functions on $[0,1]$ form a vector space under pointwise operations.
Non-example: The set of polynomials of degree exactly $2$ is not a vector space, because it does not contain $0$ and is not closed under addition.

steps: A [module](c:module) over a ring $R$ is an abelian group with a scalar multiplication by $R$ that obeys the same laws.
Take the ring $R$ to be a [field](c:field) $K$.
The module over $K$ is then a vector space, and the special case adds that every nonzero scalar has an inverse.
links.why: It shows that a vector space is a module over a field.

steps: Take a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.
Add a norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ that is positive on nonzero vectors, scales with $|a|$ and obeys the triangle inequality.
Then $V$ is a [normed space](c:normed-space).
links.why: It shows that a normed space is a vector space with a notion of length.

steps: Take a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ that is spanned by finitely many vectors.
Such a space has a finite basis, and so a dimension $n$.
Then $V$ is a [finite-dimensional vector space](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space), isomorphic to $K^n$.
links.why: It shows that finite-dimensional spaces are the vector spaces with a finite basis.

reminder: An algebraic curve is an algebraic variety of dimension one.
definition: An algebraic curve is an [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) of dimension one over a field. The zero set $\{f(x,y)=0\}$ of a nonconstant [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f$ in two variables is an example, called a plane curve.
examples: The unit circle $x^2+y^2=1$ is a plane curve.
The cubic $y^2=x^3-x$ is an elliptic curve and so an algebraic curve.
Non-example: The sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ in three-dimensional space has dimension two, so it is not a curve.

steps: Start with an [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) $X$ over a field.
Compute its dimension, which is the length of the longest chain of irreducible closed subsets.
Add the condition that this dimension is $1$; then $X$ is an algebraic curve.
links.why: It shows that a curve is a variety whose dimension is one.

steps: An [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) is a smooth projective curve of genus one with a chosen point.
It is a projective variety of dimension one.
So it is an algebraic curve, and the special case adds smoothness, genus one and the base point.
links.why: It shows that elliptic curves are algebraic curves of genus one with a base point.

reminder: A Boolean algebra is a bounded distributive lattice in which every element has a complement.
definition:
A Boolean algebra is a [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) with a least element $0$ and a greatest element $1$, in which every element $a$ has a [complement](c:complement) $
eg a$ with $a\wedge
eg a=0$ and $a\vee
eg a=1$. Its operations $\wedge$, $\vee$ and $
eg$ obey the laws of intersection, union and complement of sets.
examples: The subsets of a set $X$, with intersection, union and complement, form a Boolean algebra.
The truth values $\{0,1\}$ with and, or and not form a Boolean algebra.
The divisors of $30$, ordered by divisibility, form a Boolean algebra.
Non-example: The open subsets of $\mathbb R$ form a distributive lattice that is not Boolean, because $(0,1)$ has no complement among the open sets.

steps: Start with a [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice) that has a least element $0$ and a greatest element $1$.
Add the condition that each element $a$ has a [complement](c:complement) $b$ with $a\wedge b=0$ and $a\vee b=1$.
In a distributive lattice this complement is unique, so it defines the operation $\neg a$.
links.why: It shows that complements are the only thing a bounded distributive lattice needs to be Boolean.

steps: A [Heyting algebra](c:heyting-algebra) has an implication $a\to b$, the greatest $c$ with $a\wedge c\le b$.
In a Boolean algebra, put $a\to b=\neg a\vee b$.
This element is the greatest such $c$, so every Boolean algebra is a Heyting algebra with $\neg a=a\to0$.
links.why: It shows that classical logic is the special case of intuitionistic logic in which every element has a complement.

reminder: Two integers are coprime when their greatest common divisor is one.
definition: Integers $a$ and $b$ are coprime when their [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) is $1$, that is, when no [integer](c:integer) larger than $1$ divides both. Equivalently, $ax+by=1$ for some integers $x$ and $y$, by Bézout's identity.
examples: $8$ and $15$ are coprime, although neither of them is prime.
Any two different primes are coprime.
Two consecutive integers $n$ and $n+1$ are always coprime.
Non-example: $12$ and $18$ are not coprime, because both are divisible by $6$.

reminder: The dual space of a vector space is the vector space of all linear functionals on it.
definition: The dual space $V^*$ of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $K$ is the set of all [linear functionals](c:linear-functional) $V\to K$, with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. For a normed or topological vector space, one often keeps only the continuous functionals, which gives the continuous dual.
examples: For finite-dimensional $V$, the dual $V^*$ has the same dimension, with the dual basis $e_i^*$.
The continuous dual of a Hilbert space is isomorphic to the space itself, by the Riesz representation theorem.
Non-example: The map $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb R$ is not a linear functional, so it is not in the dual space of $\mathbb R$.

reminder: The Fréchet derivative of a map at a point is the bounded linear map that best approximates the map there.
definition: Let $f:U\to Y$ be a map from an open subset $U$ of a [normed space](c:normed-space) $X$ to a normed space $Y$. The map $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ when there is a [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator) $A:X\to Y$ with $\lVert f(x+h)-f(x)-Ah\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$ as $h\to0$, and this $A=Df(x)$ is the Fréchet derivative.
examples: For $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, the derivative $Df(x)$ is multiplication by the ordinary derivative $f'(x)$.
For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ with continuous partial derivatives, $Df(x)$ is the linear map given by the [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix).
A bounded linear operator $T$ is its own derivative at every point, $DT(x)=T$.
Non-example: The function $|x|$ on $\mathbb R$ has no Fréchet derivative at $0$, because no linear map $A$ makes $(|h|-Ah)/|h|$ tend to $0$.

steps: Take a function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and its [derivative](c:derivative) $f'(x)$ at $x$.
Let $A$ be multiplication by $f'(x)$, a bounded linear map from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$.
Then $(f(x+h)-f(x)-Ah)/h\to0$, so $Df(x)=A$.
links.why: It shows that the Fréchet derivative extends the ordinary derivative from numbers to normed spaces.

steps: Take $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ with continuous partial derivatives.
Its [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) $J$ at $x$ defines the linear map $h\mapsto Jh$.
This linear map satisfies the Fréchet condition, so $Df(x)$ is given by $J$.
links.why: It shows that in finite dimensions the Fréchet derivative is the Jacobian matrix.

reminder: A geometric series adds the terms of a sequence in which each term is a fixed multiple of the previous term.
definition: A geometric series is a [series](c:series) $\sum_{n\ge0}ar^n$ whose terms have a constant ratio $r$. Its [partial sum](c:partial-sum) is $s_n=a(1-r^{n+1})/(1-r)$ for $r\ne1$, so the series converges exactly when $|r|<1$ or $a=0$, and then its sum is $a/(1-r)$.
examples: The series $1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\cdots$ has $a=1$ and $r=\tfrac12$, and its sum is $2$.
The repeating decimal $0.333\ldots=\tfrac3{10}+\tfrac3{100}+\cdots$ is a geometric series with sum $\tfrac13$.
Non-example: The harmonic series $1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\cdots$ is not geometric, because the ratio $n/(n+1)$ of consecutive terms is not constant.

steps: Take a [series](c:series) $\sum a_n$ with terms $a_n$.
Add the condition that $a_{n+1}=ra_n$ for one fixed ratio $r$.
Then $a_n=a_0r^n$, and the series is geometric.
links.why: It shows that a geometric series is a series with a constant ratio, which is why its sum has a closed form.

steps: A [power series](c:power-series) has the form $\sum c_nx^n$.
Take all coefficients $c_n=a$.
At $x=r$ this is $\sum ar^n$, the geometric series with ratio $r$.
links.why: It shows that the geometric series is the power series with all coefficients equal.

reminder: A harmonic function is a twice differentiable function whose Laplacian is zero.
definition: A real function $u$ on an [open set](c:open-set) $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is harmonic when $u$ has continuous second [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) and its [Laplacian](c:laplace-operator) $\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial^2u/\partial x_i^2$ is $0$ on $U$. Equivalently, $u$ solves the Laplace equation $\Delta u=0$.
examples: In the plane, $u(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ is harmonic, because $\Delta u=2-2=0$.
The real part of every [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) is harmonic.
Every function $a\cdot x+b$ with a constant vector $a$ and a constant $b$ is harmonic.
Non-example: $u(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ is not harmonic, because $\Delta u=4$.

reminder: A number is the limit of a sequence when the terms eventually stay within any given distance of it.
definition: A real [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)$ has the limit $L$, a [real number](c:real-number), when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is an $N$ such that $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$. The limit is unique when it exists, and then one writes $a_n\to L$.
examples: The sequence $1/n$ has limit $0$.
The constant sequence $c,c,c,\dots$ has limit $c$.
The partial sums $1-2^{-n}$ of the series $\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}$ have limit $1$.
Non-example: The sequence $(-1)^n$ has no limit, because its terms keep jumping between $1$ and $-1$.

reminder: Vectors are linearly independent when the only linear combination of them that equals zero has all coefficients zero.
definition: A family $(v_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors in a [vector space](c:vector-space) is linearly independent when every finite [linear combination](c:linear-combination) $a_1v_{i_1}+\dots+a_kv_{i_k}=0$ with distinct indices has all coefficients $a_j=0$. Equivalently, no vector of the family is a linear combination of the others.
examples: The vectors $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are linearly independent in $\mathbb R^2$.
The monomials $1,x,x^2,\dots$ are linearly independent in the space of polynomials.
The functions $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are linearly independent in the space of real functions.
Non-example: The vectors $(1,2)$ and $(2,4)$ are dependent in $\mathbb R^2$, because $2\cdot(1,2)-(2,4)=0$.

reminder: In a normal space, any two disjoint closed sets have disjoint open neighbourhoods.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is normal when for all disjoint [closed sets](c:closed-set) $A$ and $B$ there are disjoint [open sets](c:open-set) $U\supseteq A$ and $V\supseteq B$. Some authors also require that points are closed, and call the result a $T_4$ space.
examples: Every metric space is normal.
Every compact Hausdorff space is normal.
Non-example: An infinite set with the cofinite topology is not normal, because any two nonempty open sets meet, so two disjoint nonempty finite sets cannot be separated.

steps: Take a [metrizable space](c:metrizable-space) with a metric $d$ that gives its topology, and disjoint nonempty closed sets $A$ and $B$.
Put $U=\{x : d(x,A)<d(x,B)\}$ and $V=\{x : d(x,B)<d(x,A)\}$.
These sets are open and disjoint, and they contain $A$ and $B$, so the space is normal.
links.why: It shows that every metrizable space is normal.

steps: Take disjoint closed sets $A$ and $B$ in a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space).
They are compact, and in a Hausdorff space two disjoint compact sets have disjoint open neighbourhoods.
So the space is normal.
links.why: It shows that compact Hausdorff spaces are normal.

reminder: The partial sum of a series is the sum of its terms up to a chosen index.
definition: For a [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_k)_{k\ge1}$ of numbers, the $n$th partial sum is the finite [sum](c:sum) $s_n=a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n$ for each [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$. The [series](c:series) $\sum a_k$ converges exactly when the sequence $(s_n)$ has a limit.
examples: For $a_k=k$, the partial sums are $s_1=1$, $s_2=3$, $s_3=6$ and $s_n=n(n+1)/2$.
For $a_k=2^{-k}$, the partial sums are $1-2^{-n}$, which tend to $1$.
Non-example: The infinite sum $\sum a_k$ is not a partial sum, because a partial sum adds only finitely many terms.

reminder: A rational number is a quotient of two integers with a nonzero denominator.
definition: A rational number is a number that can be written as $p/q$ with [integers](c:integer) $p$ and $q\ne0$. Two such quotients $p/q$ and $r/s$ are equal exactly when $ps=qr$.
examples: $\tfrac12$, $-\tfrac73$ and $5=\tfrac51$ are rational numbers.
Every repeating decimal is rational, for example $0.\overline{3}=\tfrac13$.
Non-example: $\sqrt2$ is not rational, because $p^2=2q^2$ has no solution in nonzero integers.

steps: Take an [integer](c:integer) $n$ and write it as $n/1$.
The quotient $n/1$ is a rational number.
So the rational numbers contain the integers and add the quotients that are not integers, such as $1/2$.
links.why: It shows that the rational numbers extend the integers by division.

steps: Take a rational number $p/q$ and view it as a point of the ordered field of [real numbers](c:real-number).
The sum, product and order of rational numbers agree with those of the real numbers.
The special case adds that the real number is a quotient $p/q$ of two integers with $q\ne0$.
links.why: It shows that the rational numbers are the real numbers that are quotients of integers.

reminder: A set of natural numbers is recursively enumerable when some algorithm lists exactly its members.
definition: A set $S\subseteq\mathbb N$ of [natural numbers](c:natural-number) is recursively enumerable when some [algorithm](c:algorithm), such as a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine), halts on input $n$ exactly when $n\in S$. Equivalently, $S$ is empty or is the range of a total [computable function](c:computable-function).
examples: The set of theorems of a computably axiomatized first-order theory is recursively enumerable.
The halting set of pairs of a machine and an input on which the machine halts is recursively enumerable.
Every [recursive set](c:recursive-subset) is recursively enumerable.
Non-example: The complement of the halting set is not recursively enumerable, because otherwise the halting set would be recursive.

steps: Take a [recursive set](c:recursive-subset) $S$, decided by an algorithm $D$ that halts on every input.
On input $n$, run $D$; if $D$ answers yes, halt, and if it answers no, loop forever.
This procedure halts exactly on the members of $S$, so $S$ is recursively enumerable.
links.why: It shows that every recursive set is recursively enumerable, and that the reverse fails for the halting set.

reminder: A solvable group has a finite chain of subgroups, each normal in the next, with abelian quotients.
definition: A [group](c:group) $G$ is solvable when there is a finite chain $1=G_0\trianglelefteq G_1\trianglelefteq\dots\trianglelefteq G_k=G$ of [subgroups](c:subgroup) in which each $G_i$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G_{i+1}$ and each [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $G_{i+1}/G_i$ is an [abelian group](c:abelian-group). Equivalently, the derived series $G\supseteq G'\supseteq G''\supseteq\cdots$ reaches $1$ after finitely many steps.
examples: Every abelian group is solvable, with the chain $1\trianglelefteq G$.
The symmetric group $S_4$ is solvable, with the chain $1\trianglelefteq V_4\trianglelefteq A_4\trianglelefteq S_4$.
Every finite $p$-group is solvable.
Non-example: The alternating group $A_5$ is not solvable, because it is simple and not abelian.

steps: Take a [nilpotent group](c:nilpotent-group) $G$ with its upper central series $1=Z_0\le Z_1\le\dots\le Z_c=G$.
Each $Z_i$ is normal in $G$, and each quotient $Z_{i+1}/Z_i$ is the center of $G/Z_i$, hence abelian.
So this chain shows that $G$ is solvable, and the special case adds that the quotients are central.
links.why: It shows that every nilpotent group is solvable, and that nilpotent groups are the solvable groups with central steps.

steps: A [metabelian group](c:metabelian-group) $G$ has an abelian normal subgroup $A$ with $G/A$ abelian.
Then $1\trianglelefteq A\trianglelefteq G$ is a chain with abelian quotients $A$ and $G/A$.
So $G$ is solvable, and the special case limits the chain to two steps.
links.why: It shows that metabelian groups are the solvable groups of derived length at most two.
